blocks.title: I Introduction
blocks.content:
The quantum electrodynamics (QED) theory predicts the
interaction between photons, wherein the collision of two real
γ photons can produce the e+e−pair, known as the linear Breit-
Wheeler (LBW) process. The LBW process is the second-order
process in QED [1], and its validation in terrestrial laborato-
ries requires an ultrahigh-brilliance γ-ray beam with a peak
cross-section of ∼1.6 × 10−29 m2 [2]. To date, the only veri-
ﬁed interaction of real photons in experiments is multiphoton
Breit-Wheeler pair production [3]. However, the production
of LBW pairs via virtual photons has been demonstrate

blocks.title: II Methods of theory and numerical simulation
blocks.content:
SIMULATION
The LBW process’s polarized scattering amplitude, with
arbitrary initial photon polarization and ﬁnal positron (elec-
tron) spins, can generally be described through the photon and
lepton density matrixes. Stokes parameters and mean spin
vectors can be utilized to describe the arbitrary polarization
states of the photon and e± in the cross section. To establish
a connection between theoretical predictions and experimen-
tal procedures, a numerical simulation method was developed
using MC sampling, which permits the consideration of beam

blocks.content:
Firstly, a clariﬁcation of the coordinate system of the LBW
process in the c.m. frame is presented in Fig. 1. In this frame,
the polar and azimuthal directions of a pair are deﬁned with
respect to the photon momentum k. Speciﬁcally, the polar
direction is given by the scattering angle θs in the scattering
plane, while the azimuthal angle ϕ is determined by p⊥in the
azimuthal plane ˆθ −ˆφ. The scattering process is thus described
in the coordinate system ( ˆo1, ˆo2, ˆo3).
